description:
We believe code can be a symbol of modern resistance. We choose exploration as our way to understand what is happening to our planet, turn knowledge into awareness, and use technology to make a difference.

We're looking for curious minds who want to explore, create, and make an impact together.

Skills we're looking for: Software Development, UI/UX Design, Storytelling, and Earth Science.
summary:
Eyes on Karhutla turns 14 years of NASA fire detections into a consistent history of forest and land fire activity (karhutla) across Indonesia. MODIS and VIIRS can't simply be combined. VIIRS has finer pixels and is more sensitive, so it records about 5.5 times as many detections as MODIS. That ratio also swings from 2.4× to 12× from day to day. Merging their hotspots makes fire activity seem to jump whenever a new satellite launches.

We built an open, tested Python pipeline that puts both sensors on one shared unit, the active cell-day: a 0.01° grid cell (about 1 km) with at least one detection on a given Indonesian Western Time (WIB) calendar date. It reports MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP side by side for every province from 2012 to 2026, and never adds them together. Every date is marked complete, partial or missing, so a gap in the data is never shown as a quiet day.

A public bilingual web map (Indonesian and English) lets anyone explore the history by province, year and sensor, see where the sensors agree, and share or cite any view. Indonesia burns again every dry season. Researchers, journalists and policymakers need fire history they can compare across years and trust, and that is what this provides.
details:
What it does and how it works

The project has two parts in one repository.

1. Scientific pipeline (Python). All the calculation happens here, in six steps:

- Ingestion: pulls the NASA FIRMS standard-processing (science-quality) archive for MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) over Indonesia, from 2012 to mid-2026.

- Preprocessing: puts all sensors into one data format. Invalid rows are removed with a recorded reason, never silently.

- Harmonization: keeps only vegetation-fire detections (FIRMS type = 0). Each one is placed on a 0.01° grid and assigned a WIB calendar date. The output is "active cell-days", with flags showing which satellites saw each one.

- Regions: assigns each cell-day to one of Indonesia's 34 provinces. Detections outside every province are reported separately, not dropped.

- Activity: builds daily, monthly and yearly series for MODIS (Terra + Aqua) and VIIRS S-NPP. Each series uses a fixed set of satellites, so adding a new satellite can't create a fake trend.

- Export: writes versioned JSON/GeoJSON files with JSON Schemas. Nothing is written unless every schema check passes and the totals agree across files (Indonesia equals the sum of the provinces; yearly totals equal the sum of the daily and monthly values).

2. Public web map (TypeScript, React, MapLibre). It reads the exported files and validates them when they load. It only displays data and never calculates figures. Features:

- a province map coloured by one sensor at a time;

- active cells as dots, coloured by sensor agreement (MODIS only, VIIRS only, or both);

- each cell's detection dates for each sensor;

- a year picker and a monthly chart covering 2012–2026;

- shareable links and a citation that records which data export and pipeline version you viewed;

- notes on what the metric means and where the data has gaps.

The harmonization finding that shaped the design

We tested the 2019 fire season, about 800,000 detections. VIIRS saw about 5.6 times as many active cell-days as MODIS, ranging from 2.4× to 12.2×. This stayed true on grids up to 0.1°, so the difference comes from VIIRS's higher sensitivity, not its smaller pixels. The daily pattern still matched closely (correlation of about 0.92). A single conversion factor would therefore be misleading. We chose a common unit plus side-by-side series with fixed satellites, which is honest and reproducible. Calibrating the sensors against each other in years when both operate is the planned next step.

Benefits and intended impact

- A comparable fire history: seasons and years can be compared fairly, from the 2015 and 2019 crises to quieter years, without false jumps when satellites change.

- Trust through transparency: coverage gaps, partial periods, what the metric means and sensor provenance are all visible. Every number traces back to source record IDs. Hotspots are always described as detections of heat, not confirmed fires.

- Citable and reproducible: every map view is a link, and citations record the data version.

- Accessible: Indonesian is the default language, alongside English. Nothing to install, no account, and no paid map service.

- Intended users: researchers, journalists, NGOs, local governments and residents who want to understand seasonal and recurring burning patterns per province.

Tools, languages and software

- Languages: Python 3.12 and TypeScript.

- Data processing: pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, requests.

- Data contract between the two parts: JSON Schema, jsonschema, Ajv, json-schema-to-typescript (TypeScript types are generated from the pipeline's schemas).

- Research and internal tools: JupyterLab, Streamlit, Plotly, Folium.

- Web: React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, OpenFreeMap basemap, uPlot charts.

- Testing and quality: pytest, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright, oxlint.

- Tooling: uv, npm, Git and GitHub.

- Hardware: standard laptops only, no special hardware. The full 2012–2026 export takes about 4 minutes.

- AI-assisted development: written with AI coding assistants under documented project rules (AGENTS.md and a "Lode" knowledge base of design decisions).

How it's creative

- It treats harmonization as a scientific question, not a merge. When the data showed the sensors can't be reliably converted into each other, we chose to show that honestly instead of hiding it.

- Sensor agreement is mapped: you can see where MODIS and VIIRS both saw a cell and where only one did.

- "Missing is never zero" is enforced everywhere, from the data files to the chart.

- A strict data contract: the web app refuses data that fails validation, so wrong numbers never reach the map.

- Every map view is citable, linking public exploration back to a specific data version.

Factors the team considered

- Sensor differences: pixel size (about 1 km vs. 375 m), confidence scales that don't match, overpass times, and when each satellite started (MODIS 2000, S-NPP 2012, NOAA-20 2018, NOAA-21 2023).

- Time zones: a single national calendar date in WIB, with partial dates at the edges of each data pull flagged.

- Scientific honesty: a detection is not a fire, a burned area or a measure of intensity, and the app says so.

- Existing systems: Indonesia already runs SiPongi+, the Ministry of Forestry's fire information platform. We focused on cross-sensor harmonization and long-term history rather than rebuilding a live hotspot map.

- Licensing and attribution: NASA FIRMS, geoBoundaries/OpenStreetMap (ODbL 1.0) and OpenFreeMap are credited in the app.

- Known limitations, stated openly:

- boundaries show the 34 provinces of 2017, not today's 38;

- the archive data has a delay, and near-real-time data is excluded on purpose;

- possible orbit drift of the aging Terra and Aqua satellites still needs checking.

- Future work:

- flagging unusual fire activity against a historical baseline;

- calibrating the sensors against each other in years when both operate;

- automated data publishing;

- a moderated layer for community reports, kept clearly separate from satellite data.
